    init:

      load_let_values
      call Someroutine

    ...
    ...
    ...

      letb bits_x,62
      letb bits_y,56

      lds r16,bits_x

    Etc.

As soon as you have something larger than the hardware atomic size (or unaligned in memory) you risk torn reads/writes. So a pointer + a size for example on some architectures (some hardware like x86 has a double word atomic support, but on embedded you usually only get up to word size atomics).

All this means that you can't (in a systems level language) feasibly make everything atomic and ensure no UB.

All that said, do I wish Rust did more for other concurrency bugs? Yes, sure. Though there is some hope: I have seen Rust crates to enforce lock ordering at compile time (I think that originally came out of the Fuchsia OS kernel development). There is also scoped threads, rayon, actor frameworks etc. All different approaches to strucured concurrency, with the goal of reducing bugs. Different frameworks seem to suit different problems though. For what I do I rarely need mutexes, instead either rayon or message passing work well.

> First, one question arises: what are the 12 million lines doing if they're not needed? Secondly, don't those 12 million lines build up the theory that is eventually proved? Mistakes could be there that makes the outer statement seem like something it isn't, could there not be?

This seems to reflect an incorrect understanding of formal mathematics.

Formal mathematics can be thought of as a game with rules where a statement to be proved is some game end state. If you play 12 million valid moves and arrive at the desired end state then you have proved that the statement is valid. If your logical system is sound (e.g. first order logic), then you have proved your statement is true.

The entire point of the formalization of logic and mathematics through the 19th and 20th centuries was to unlock this capability. Such that, if you only care about whether your statement is true or not and not why it's true, the intermediate steps are entirely unnecessary.

To answer each of your questions:

> First, one question arises: what are the 12 million lines doing if they're not needed?

They are the intermediate computations necessary to show that the final statement is valid. This is much like intermediate arithmetic operations in a large complicated arithmetic expression. As long as you believe that the computer can calculate each individual arithmetic expression correctly, you don't need to manually review the billions of intermediate calculations that result in the final number.

> Secondly, don't those 12 million lines build up the theory that is eventually proved?

No. Not in the way you're thinking of. It seems you are using "theory" to mean the concepts necessary to express the statement itself. This is a very different set of lines than the proof itself (and generally much much more compact). Very difficult to prove statements can be stated in very simple language. Often the theory is <0.01% of the total lines of code.

> Mistakes could be there that makes the outer statement seem like something it isn't, could there not be?

No. Only the language used in the final statement can cause this issue, i.e. the theory. The intermediate 12 million lines cannot affect this, assuming your computer can carry out arithmetic correctly.

Another way of thinking about it is that the big breakthrough of 19th and 20th century mathematical logic is to conclusively show that formal mathematics is fundamentally just a set of arithmetic operations.

Hence in a very real sense, proving a mathematical statement is exactly identical to finding x in an arithmetic expression f with some constant k such that f(x) = k, where k is determined by the statement you wish to prove (not the 12 million lines).

Showing that x causes f(x) to equal k is exactly equivalent to proving the mathematical statement associated with k.

The 12 million lines are an alternative notation, no different in spirit to decimal notation or binary notation, of writing down x. It is some gigantic natural number.

You must understand k. If you use the wrong k, then you have proved another statement than what you intended. This is usually about a dozen lines of code.

You must be confident in the correctness of f. This corresponds to the believing that your type checker (since Lean uses dependent typing as its method of proof checking) has no fundamental soundness bugs. This can be controversial and indeed Lean's type checker has had soundness bugs in the past! But crucially f does not depend on k or x. Every time you fix a bug in f you can rerun it for any k or x you care about.

But you don't have to actually read all the digits of x, in whatever notation you care about. You can copy paste it in from some gigantic file handed to you by a stranger. As long as f(x) = k, you know that you have proved the mathematical statement associated with k.

Overall, this is roughly like asking why you trust a computer to solve a long division problem that has 12 million intermediate steps if you don't actually read all 12 million intermediate steps yourself. Well I trust the computer to do one step of division correctly and to be able to repeat that faithfully 12 million times. Hence I trust the computer can solve a long division problem involving millions of digits, even if I don't actually look at all 12 million intermediate computations myself.
